: > In the advanced game, there is *no* explicit statement of

: > rules on this (that I could find anyway), only an example.

This is where splitting VAMPIRE into the basic and advanced (Jyhad)
variants was an extremely short sighted idea. Dumbing down and making
conflicting rules within supposedly the same game was wrong.

I highly suggest you get ahold of an OLD Jyhad rulebook and use the
errata in the Duelist and from this newsgroup to augment it. Also, never
play the "basic" game. The complexity and interaction and ability of
vampires to come back after getting stomped into topor is what makes it
so challenging and fun.

Messages.Author: Jeremy York
Messages.Body:
Graham H. Watt (g...@saba.kuentos.guam.net) wrote:

: : > In the advanced game, there is *no* explicit statement of

: : > rules on this (that I could find anyway), only an example.

: This is where splitting VAMPIRE into the basic and advanced (Jyhad)
: variants was an extremely short sighted idea. Dumbing down and making
: conflicting rules within supposedly the same game was wrong.

I think it's more a matter of bad editing. Nothing inherently bad
about breaking the rules into two chunks, as long as it's done so that
there aren't any conflicting rules between the two. And so that
the reader is prepared for the changes on their way in the standard game.
WotC did ok but not great on this latter point. On the former point,
since Tom has stated this rulebook eratta, there aren't really any
"conflicting" rules between the two (I'd call burning vamps instead of
toporizing them, and not allowing press/maneuver/intercept, "simplifications"
rather than conflicting rules).

And there *is* value to the basic game; I'm going to teach the game to some
friends who are not hard-core gamers by any means, and playing the basic
game once with them will help them master some of the essential stuff
before we make the plunge into the full-blown game.

The criticism I would level against how the game was split into a basic
and advanced game, is that the guidelines on which cards to leave
out are pretty weak. "If you don't understand it, leave it out" just
doesn't cut the mustard...I went through a set of cold Jyhad decks I use to
teach people the game, and there were quite a few cards that I pulled
because either they were useless (in the basic game) or had stuff buried
in the fine print that would make them inappropriate for the basic game.

What is needed is either a list of cards to leave out or some kind
of marking on the cards themselves to indicate whether they should be
used in the basic game. Not having these makes it harder for the new
player to sit down with their cards and learn the basics...and wasn't
that the whole idea of the basic game?

: I highly suggest you get ahold of an OLD Jyhad rulebook and use the

: errata in the Duelist and from this newsgroup to augment it.

*shrug* I have plenty of old rulebooks, but doubt that I'll ever give
them another look, except to figure out whether something's changed. The
current book is the one that WotC supports, so I'll stick with that, thanks.

: Also, never

: play the "basic" game. The complexity and interaction and ability of
: vampires to come back after getting stomped into topor is what makes it
: so challenging and fun.

I will play the basic game if I'm teaching the game to someone. My
first couple of games of Jyhad were somewhat bewildering, and I had read
the rulebook cover to cover in advance. I made it just fine, but
then I'm a hard core gamer. Some of the people I'd like to teach the
game to are not. And the rules that allow that complexity and interaction
might be daunting to them at first.

So, I wouldn't say "never play the basic game"...I'd say "don't bother
playing it more than once or twice (unless of course you're using it
to teach the game to others).
